intro: You're looking for an equity release adviser near you because you want to understand whether releasing money from your home could work for your later-life plans. Perhaps you're thinking about topping up your retirement income, helping family, or covering a large expense. A local adviser can explain the options in person and help you weigh up the decision.
need_heading: What people searching for an equity release adviser near me usually need
need_lead: Most people want clear, face-to-face advice about how equity release works and whether it fits their circumstances.
needs: You may be considering a lifetime mortgage to supplement your pension income and want to know how the interest and repayments would work.
You might be thinking about a home reversion plan and need to understand how selling a share of your home affects your future.
You could be worried about leaving enough for your family and want to explore how equity release might affect your estate.
You may have a specific expense in mind, such as home improvements or helping a family member, and want to see if equity release is suitable.
You might be comparing equity release with downsizing or other later-life borrowing and need help understanding the trade-offs.
context_heading: Understanding equity release advice and regulation
context: Equity release advice is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), and advisers must hold a specialist qualification. You can check the firm on the FCA register. Most providers and advisers are members of the Equity Release Council, whose standards include a no-negative-equity promise and the right to stay in your home for life.

You will also need your own solicitor to explain the legal documents before you sign. Many advisers encourage you to involve family members in the discussion, so it can help to have a relative with you at appointments.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Mention that you are looking for an equity release adviser near you and give your town or postcode so we can introduce you to a suitable professional.
Explain what you hope to achieve with equity release, such as boosting your income or covering a specific cost.
Let us know if you have a particular type of plan in mind, like a lifetime mortgage or home reversion plan.
Tell us if you have already discussed equity release with family or a solicitor, as this can affect what you need.
Share any concerns you have about fees, interest rates, or moving home in the future.
Mention if you would prefer to meet in person or are happy with telephone or video advice.
questions: Are you and your firm regulated by the FCA and listed on the FCA register?
Are you a member of the Equity Release Council and what standards does that commit you to?
How do you compare a lifetime mortgage with a home reversion plan for my situation?
What are the total costs involved, including any arrangement fees, valuation fees, and legal fees?
What happens if I want to move home or repay the plan early?
How will equity release affect what I can leave to my family, and can I protect some of my estate?

faqs.q: Do I need to use an adviser near me?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but a local adviser can meet you face to face and may have a better understanding of property values in your area. Many advisers also offer telephone or video appointments, so you can choose what suits you.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a lifetime mortgage and a home reversion plan?
faqs.a: A lifetime mortgage is a loan secured against your home where you retain ownership, while a home reversion plan involves selling a share of your home for a lump sum or regular income. An adviser can explain the pros and cons of each.

faqs.q: Will equity release affect my benefits or tax position?
faqs.a: Equity release can affect means-tested benefits, and the money released is generally tax-free but may affect your estate for inheritance tax. It's important to discuss your circumstances with the adviser and possibly a benefits adviser or tax specialist.

faqs.q: Can I involve my family in the decision?
faqs.a: Yes, many advisers encourage you to involve family members, and you can bring them to appointments. It can be helpful to have a relative with you to ask questions and understand the long-term implications.

extra_heading: Choosing between local advisers and weighing up what you're offered
extra: Searching for an adviser near you often means you'd rather sit down with someone and talk it through, but it's worth asking upfront whether the first meeting happens at their office, in your home, or by phone or video. A local firm may know your area's property values well, yet the advice itself should follow the same regulated standards wherever the adviser is based.

When you compare what different advisers tell you, look at how clearly they explain both the benefits and the drawbacks of releasing money from your home, and whether they set out alternatives such as downsizing or other later-life borrowing. Ask whether they advise across the whole market or from a limited panel, since that shapes what you'll be shown. Fees are usually price on application, so ask for the total cost in writing before you commit to anything.

It also helps to check that the firm appears on the FCA register and that the adviser holds the specialist qualification equity release advice requires. Membership of the Equity Release Council is worth confirming too, as its standards include the right to stay in your home for life and a no-negative-equity promise. Bring a relative or friend to the first appointment if you can, and have your questions about moving home, repaying early and your estate ready.

extra_faqs.q: Should I choose an adviser who is close by, or does distance matter less than I think?
extra_faqs.a: Being nearby can make face-to-face meetings easier, especially if you'd like the adviser to visit you at home. But the quality of the advice matters more than the postcode, so it's fine to consider an adviser further away if they explain things in a way you understand and meet the same regulatory standards.

extra_faqs.q: What should I have ready for a first meeting with a local equity release adviser?
extra_faqs.a: It helps to know the rough value of your home, any outstanding mortgage or secured borrowing, and what you'd like the released money to do. Bring details of your income and any benefits you receive, plus a note of your questions, and consider asking a family member to come with you.

extra_faqs.q: If an adviser visits me at home, does that change anything about the advice?
extra_faqs.a: The setting shouldn't change the standards the advice has to meet, as equity release advice is regulated by the FCA wherever it takes place. What matters is that you understand the recommendation, have time to think, and still get your own solicitor to explain the legal documents before you sign.
